title: A holy man at the door
hookLine: a holy man at the door, a seat and water, and then a name
carry: the robe doesn't make the sannyasi
tomorrow: Sita calls the forest to witness

lines: A HOLY MAN ON THE PATH.
cards: The hut at Panchavati is quiet. Rama is gone after the deer, Lakshmana gone after Rama. Then someone comes up the path: a wandering holy man.
Valmiki dresses him carefully: a saffron robe, a tuft of hair, an umbrella, sandals, a staff and a water pot. Every detail says safe. Then the poet tells what the forest knows and Sita doesn't.
The trees stop stirring. The wind drops. The Godavari, watching him, slows its current in fear.

teach.b: Sita does what a good forest household would do. She greets the guest, offers him a seat and water for his feet, and tells him food is ready. Atithi devo bhava, the guest is God, and a wandering ascetic most of all.
He asks who she is, and she answers straight: her father Janaka, her husband Rama, the exile. She even asks his name.
Then the mask slips. Ravana, lord of Lanka, the one even the gods fear. He praises her beauty and offers her palaces and the place of his chief queen.
Leave this forest, he says, and this man who has lost his kingdom. Sita is alone, and she does not flinch.
Rama is a lion, she says, and you're a jackal hoping for a lioness. He's the ocean; you're a trickle. Taking her would be like pulling a tooth from a lion's mouth.
Now see what Ravana has done. In Hindu life the saffron robe of a sannyasi, a renunciant, is honored because it says: I've given up taking. That's why households feed renunciants.
Ravana puts on one of the most honored dresses in Hindu life to do the worst taking of all. The tradition has an old answer.

teach.h: THE GITA: LETTING GO MAKES THE SANNYASI.
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the true sannyasi isn't the one who merely gives up the sacred fire and the rites, but the one who does the work to be done without grasping at its fruit.

teach.h: THE ROBE DOESN'T MAKE THE SANNYASI.
teach.b: The robe doesn't make the sannyasi. So Sita's welcome isn't the mistake, and Valmiki doesn't blame her for it. The lie is all Ravana's.
And her words don't stop him.

how: Honoring guests (atithi devo bhava, from the Taittiriya Upanishad) and feeding renunciants are old Hindu ideals, and tellers of the Ramayana do not blame Sita for welcoming the guest. The Gita (6.1) places renunciation in letting go, not in the robe.

o: Ravana's carrying off of Sita, begun with a disguise
a duel between Ravana and Lakshmana at the hut
Rama's rescue of Sita from a rakshasa in the forest

games.q: at the hut — tap the pairs.
p: a seat and water for the feet
Rama and Ravana, in Sita's words

s: Sita is tricked because she is foolish
she does what a good household does for a guest; Valmiki puts the fault on the disguise.
Valmiki puts the fault on Ravana's lie, not on Sita's welcome
her kindness is real; the disguise is what's false.
in Hindu teaching, wearing the saffron robe is what makes someone a sannyasi
the Gita places it in letting go. Ravana wears the robe and is the opposite.

games.q: a wandering sadhu stops at your temple and asks for a meal. after today's story, what do you do?
o: feed him: honoring renunciants is still dharma, and Ravana's lie doesn't change that.
turn him away; Sita's story shows you can't trust any sadhu.
feed him only if he can prove he is holy first.
games.why: Valmiki blames the disguise, not the welcome. Hindus keep honoring guests and renunciants; the lie belongs to the liar.

practice: Many Hindu homes still offer water to anyone who comes in, the first gift to a guest. If you can, pour a glass of water and set it out, as if someone were arriving. As you pour, think: the guest is God.
Then picture Sita at the door: the open hand that welcomes, and the straight back that can still say no. Hindu welcome holds both. Sit with the glass for a few slow breaths.

wordCard.voice: The abduction. It begins with a renunciant's robe and a guest's welcome, and it meets Sita's refusal: a lion, and a jackal.

orig.note: Sanskrit parivrājaka: a wandering ascetic, one who goes around. the form Ravana takes to reach Sita.

carryVoice: Your line: the robe doesn't make the sannyasi. Tomorrow, the disguise falls away completely. Day five hundred seventy-two, done.
